bp: The real object in this paper is a short-video feed where each open of the app becomes a fast sequence of choices. The system has millions of videos it could show, but it can show only a few, and each user may change direction quickly. A person may watch several videos in one mood, then move to another topic minutes later. Researchers who want to improve this kind of feed need records that look like the real setting: many users, many videos, repeated interactions over time, different kinds of feedback, and context around the viewing moment. The paper argues that this evidence has been missing in public form. VK-LSVD is offered as an industrial short-video dataset with over 40 billion interactions from 10 million users and almost 20 million videos across six months. Its purpose is not just to publish a large table; it is to make realistic study possible for sequential recommendation, cold-start cases, and short-video systems.
wh: The difficulty begins with speed and partial evidence. In short-video recommendation, the system rarely gets a clean statement of what the user wants. It mostly sees traces left by behavior, and the abstract explicitly calls this implicit feedback. Those traces are useful, but they are noisy because a behavior can have several meanings. A user may pass a video because it is irrelevant, because the moment is wrong, or because another video pulled attention away. The user interest can also shift rapidly, so yesterday's or even earlier-session behavior may not describe the current need. A second difficulty is research access. If only private platforms hold realistic logs, public research can overfit to small or artificial collections that do not contain the same scale, churn, cold-start pressure, or platform dynamics. The paper is hard because it tries to expose enough real industrial structure for useful research while still packaging the data into an open dataset that others can analyze and compare against.
naive: A smart beginner would start with a smaller public recommendation dataset, count which users interacted with which videos, and train a model to show more of what each user previously liked. That first attempt is reasonable because recommendation often begins from repeated behavior. It fails here because short-video feeds are more time-sensitive and more context-sensitive than a static user-item table. If the data is too small, it may not contain enough new videos, rare interests, or fast changes to test whether a method handles real feed pressure. If it has only one feedback type, it cannot show how different user reactions tell different stories. If it lacks context or content information, it cannot support cold-start research where a new video has little interaction history but still has observable properties.
ap: The core idea is to make the dataset itself carry the missing structure of the real problem. VK-LSVD gathers a very large interaction record from an industrial short-video platform: over 40 billion interactions, 10 million users, almost 20 million videos, and six months of activity. The paper then enriches that interaction record with several kinds of evidence. It includes content embeddings, meaning precomputed numeric summaries of video content that let a system compare videos by what they contain rather than only by who watched them. It includes diverse feedback signals, so the record is not reduced to a single yes-or-no click. It also includes contextual metadata, so the viewing event is tied to surrounding conditions rather than treated as an isolated mark. The move is therefore to turn recommendation research from a toy pile of interactions into an open, large-scale, time-aware, multi-signal record that can support realistic tests.
mech: The mechanism starts with platform activity over six months. The raw ingredients are users, videos, interaction events, video-related content descriptions, multiple feedback signals, and contextual metadata. First, each event ties a user to a video at a point in the viewing history. This matters because sequential recommendation needs order: the system must know not only what a user touched, but what came before what. Second, the dataset keeps video-side evidence. The abstract names content embeddings; in plain language, these are compact numeric descriptions produced from the video content so that a new or rarely viewed video is not invisible just because few people have interacted with it. Third, the dataset keeps more than one feedback signal. That lets researchers study whether different reactions provide stronger, weaker, or differently timed evidence about preference. Fourth, contextual metadata gives the event more surroundings, which can matter when the same user behaves differently across situations. Fifth, the authors analyze the dataset's quality and diversity, which is necessary because a large log is useful only if it is not a narrow or broken sample. Finally, the output is an open resource used to build realistic benchmarks, meaning shared test settings where methods can be compared on the same evidence, including sequential recommendation and cold-start scenarios. Its role in the live VK RecSys Challenge 2025 is presented as immediate evidence that the dataset can support real community use.
math: The main mathematical ideas are sequences, ranking, similarity, sampling, and uncertainty from observed behavior. Sequence reasoning treats a user's history as an ordered record, not a bag of unrelated events. The question is which earlier interactions still matter for the next video and which have gone stale. Ranking turns candidate videos into an order, because the feed can show only a small slice of almost 20 million videos. Similarity enters through content embeddings, unpacked as numeric summaries that make videos comparable by content. The useful operation is measuring nearness: if two videos have similar content descriptions, evidence from one may help reason about the other, especially when one is new. Probability is present in the background because implicit feedback does not state preference directly; it changes the system's belief about what the user may want. Dataset quality also has a mathematical side. A large public dataset must preserve enough variety across users, videos, time, feedback, and context so that conclusions are not artifacts of a tiny sample. The central tradeoff is realism versus control: real industrial logs contain scale and messiness, while shared benchmarks need stable definitions so methods can be compared fairly.
dots: This paper sits in the recommender-systems part of the conference, but its deeper connection is to the shared problem of choosing a small useful set from a huge, changing pile. It links directly to sequence papers because short-video interest is described as rapidly shifting, so order and recency matter. It links to cold-start recommendation because almost 20 million videos means many items will have little behavioral history at some point, forcing systems to use content and context rather than only past popularity. It links to ranking because every recommender ultimately sorts candidate videos for limited feed positions. It also links to evaluation and benchmarking work: before researchers can argue that one method is better, they need a shared setting whose data resembles the deployment pressure. VK-LSVD therefore plays a connective role. It is not another scoring method; it is infrastructure for testing many scoring methods under a more realistic short-video setting.
ww: The dataset should help because it matches the shape of the problem better than the naive research setup. If the real system contains fast interest shifts, then six months of ordered interactions gives researchers a way to study remembering and forgetting over time. If implicit feedback is ambiguous, then diverse feedback signals give more evidence than a single interaction label, while still leaving room to test how each signal should be interpreted. If new videos are common, then content summaries and contextual metadata provide information before enough interaction history accumulates. If scale changes behavior, then 40 billion interactions from 10 million users and almost 20 million videos can reveal long-tail patterns, sparse cases, and platform dynamics that small collections may hide. The paper's analysis of quality and diversity matters for the same reason: size alone is not enough. The dataset works as a research object only if it contains varied, coherent evidence that can stand in for the pressures of an operating short-video platform.
po: The payoff is an open industrial-scale resource for a field where realistic public data has been scarce. Researchers can use VK-LSVD to build and compare methods for sequential recommendation, where recent behavior changes the next suggestion, and for cold-start scenarios, where new or rarely seen videos need to be recommended without much history. The abstract grounds the scale claim in concrete numbers: over 40 billion interactions, 10 million users, almost 20 million videos, and six months of activity. It also says the dataset already has practical community uptake through the live VK RecSys Challenge 2025. The gain is better evidence for studying next-generation short-video recommenders.
limits: The abstract does not prove that VK-LSVD represents every short-video platform, country, creator ecosystem, or user group. It says the analysis supports quality and diversity, but the details of that analysis are not in the provided input. The usefulness of content embeddings depends on whether those numeric content summaries preserve the video features that matter for recommendation. The usefulness of feedback signals depends on whether researchers interpret them carefully rather than treating every action as a clean preference label. The dataset also supports benchmarks, but a benchmark is only a controlled proxy for deployment. Real feeds still involve policy choices, changing trends, creator incentives, and user welfare questions that the abstract does not settle.
